utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. There are three matters to deal with before we proceed to hear evidence today. The first thing relates to the 17th motion for finding of disclosure violation. The Chamber notes the request filed by the accused on 23rd September 2010 for leave replay to the 17th motion. Having considered the 17th motion and Prosecution's response to the 17th motion and the request for leave to reply, the Chamber is satisfied that it has enough information to make an informed decision on -- on the motion. Therefore, it follows that any further response by the accused is unnecessary, and it would not be in the interest of justice to hear that response. Accordingly, the accused's request for leave to reply is denied. The second matter relates to the binding order motion against Canada. As you are well aware, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, Canada is in the process of seeking permission from a third state to produce to you one remaining document relating to your request. You have requested the Chamber that it give Canada a dead-line of 1st of October, 2010, for the production of that one document. Before the Chamber proceeds to deal with your -- that request, I would like to know if there's been any developments or correspondence between the Defence and Canada since Defence has made its request. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There's been no word from Canada since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. For the last matter, I'd like to go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could I say something briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. Please do accept the assurances of my consideration. However, with all due respect to all the participants involved, the subject matter that the next witness will be dealing with, namely, incidents that are being confirmed through him, require a great deal more time. In every country that has ever heard in democracy and that has any kind of a judicial system, every one of these incidents would have taken at least two days of trial time. According to the current decision of the Trial Chamber, I have only 15 minutes respectively to deal with each and every one of these incidents. I know that you're generous. When the examination is moving on properly, you do give me more time. However, there should be a decision as well. From the very outset the decision should show full understanding for the needs of the Defence, namely to shed more light on these incidents. Once more light is shed on them, which is quite possible, they will look completely different. So please do reconsider your basic decision on the time allocated to the Defence for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber considered the limited scope of the testimony of the next witness, in particular that the -- all analyses are related to the same sorts of sniping incidents, and the logic used in the analysis is not very different in each case. Therefore, the Chamber is not minded to reconsider the time limit for cross-examination, which is set for -- as four hours at this moment. Let the witness be brought in. You know, of course, depending upon the efficiency and relevance of your cross-examination, there's room for further extension; but at this moment the Chamber is of the view that four hours is more than sufficient at this moment. You'll have more time with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting, turning back to the issue of leave to reply to the 17th disclosure motion, our team spent this week going over those 6.000 documents that you gave us the time to review, and we found 96 violations of Rule 68. Would it be inappropriate if we simply supplied the Chamber a table listing the documents with the violation so that you could know that information when determining the scope of the violations that underlie that motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no reason not to grant it, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll file that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: My name is Patrick van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you are of Dutch nationality?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've provided a CV to the Prosecution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask that 14046 be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, since you provided your CV to the Prosecution you have returned to the Dutch armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you currently hold the rank of captain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you see the document on the screen in front you. Is that your CV?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It appears from your CV that you initially trained as a sharpshooter and then trained as a sniper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you explain briefly the difference between a sharpshooter and a sniper?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The sniper will have had the same -- the same training that a sharpshooter has had but he will have more advanced technical training as well in addition to the technical part of shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What would the technical aspect of the training encompass?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: To be able to operate as a two-man team or a three-man team and plan their own missions and execute their missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've also undertaken training as a sniper instructor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What would a course in sniper instruction encompass?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It usually runs parallel to a sniper course and is intended to train snipers to be able to train other snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At this stage, I'd request that the CV be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1611; Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Van der Weijden, you've prepared a report for the Trial Chamber in which you provided your opinion on the origin of fire and the weapon used and the opportunity which the shooter might have had to identify the target in relation to a number of incidents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 14045, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, is that the front page of your report you see?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It is the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the witness please be asked to pause before answering so that there could be a pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Van der Weijden, probably my fault. I'll try and leave a pause myself. Mr. Van der Weijden, your report is essentially divided into two parts, a general part and a specific analysis of a number of incidents. I want to first ask you a number of questions about the general part. Now, in your report you describe the importance of training, and you've already discussed the training which you yourself underwent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At this stage I'd like to ask for document 20831, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document which you are about to see is an order signed by General Dragomir Milosevic of the SRK command, dated January 1995. It's entitled "Order to training SRK units in 1995." And I'd like to take you, Mr. Van der Weijden, to page 6 in the English, which is the 8th page in the B/C/S. Just look at the first paragraph of that document, Mr. Van der Weijden. It states: "A course for sniper instructors will start on 23rd January 1995 in the Jahorina Barracks sector and last eight days. Course commander and training instructor Captain Terzic as per attachment 7." Do you have any observations on that entry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, it would be, of course, a course of sniper instructors which I assume would be taught to people that are very -- already on the ground sniper training, and it will last eight days, which is rather a short time for such a course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Nevertheless, could you give some idea as to what subjects might have been covered in such a course, based on your own experience.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I presume, if it is a sniper instructor course, the course will at least be about the subject of shooting or precision shooting, some technical training or how to provide the technical training for the snipers and -- but I think one of the main subjects will also be how to deploy the snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1612, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like to request document 15602, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. Van der Weijden, is an order signed by General Dragomir Milosevic of the SRK command. It's dated the 19th of January, 1995. It's addressed to a number of units, including, among others, the Igman Infantry Brigade. Now, if you could look at the document on your screen, and, as we can see, the first three paragraphs essentially deal with the logistics of transporting sniper instructors out of various units to the Jahorina Barracks. Could you focus on paragraph 4. Have a read of paragraph 4, and give us your observations on that, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, the instructors are required to take their personal weapons. And since their weapons are M-76, which is the -- the standard sniper rifle of the JNA, was the standard sniper rifle of the JNA, I assume they would already have to be snipers, so -- in order to become sniper instructors. And in addition to -- to the weapons, they will also have to bring equipment to -- to winter conditions on the mountain which might be just warm clothing but also camouflage equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1613, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I now request that 65 ter 15405 be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This next document is a communication from Major Ljubisa Petricevic of the command of the 1st Igman Infantry Brigade to the SRK command, dated the 15th of January, 1995. And on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could have the English, please, as well. There's no English available for that at the moment. I have an English translation here. Perhaps we can return to that document a little later. Thank you. Now I'd like document 12206 to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document which is coming up now is dated the 14th of August, 1994, and it's signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Sehovac, and it is from the command of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, and it is issued to the command in this instance of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. Now, I'd like to take you to the second page of the document in English, to item number 12. Now, you said in your report that snipers in NATO armies - this was at page 3 of your report - are usually organised in separate platoons at the battalion level. Does this document enable you to comment on how snipers might have been organised in the VRS, in the Bosnian Serb Army, that is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to exactly conclude it, but from -- from 12 I would conclude that the snipers are deemed as an important asset for the commanders, because they're placed on the same level as machine-gun or heavy machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you have any comments about the reference to sighted enemy targets in the area of defence -- in the areas of defence, correction.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I might be able to conclude that they are -- the snipers, the machine-guns, and the Browning gunners are to fire at -- are -- they will have to fire at the sight of enemy targets. So if there are targets that would present themselves in -- in their area, they would have to fire on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is there any clarification as to what an enemy targets consists of in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that that be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document has already been admitted; it's P1208. It's also 65 ter 12202.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document in front of us now is also from Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sehovac to a number of battalions; in this case, the command of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. Now, I'd like to focus your attention on the third paragraph of this document, Mr. Van der Weijden, and you see there there's a reference to "paired snipers." Could you enlighten us as to what the reference to "paired snipers" is there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: A sniper might be able to operate alone, but usually, as I'm used to, a sniper will use -- will work as a sniper pair in which one of the snipers who are both sniper trained will act as the spotter. So he will not have -- he might have a precision rifle, but he will not use it at that time, but he will be working with high-magnification optics to support the shooter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 4 of that document, it states that: "Snipers should be given precise tasks: place, time, mode of combat, mode of combat control, and a method of reporting the results. In combat, use primarily weapons with silencers and shoot with precision (use ammunition sparingly)." Could you comment on that entry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, the first sentence would -- is -- it amplifies the importance of the -- of the snipers because they're given -- for a single man to be given place, time, mode of combat, mode of combat control, and a method, it's structurised. And for the second sentence, to use weapons with silencers, well personally I don't think silencers is the correct term; it would be a suppressor. But a suppressor on a rifle lessens the profile of the shot. So there is less muzzle flash, less blast, less sound, which helps to disguise the sniper. And to shoot with precision and use ammunition sparingly would imply that the good ammunition was difficult to get. So they would have to be more economical with their ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now back to the document which we were trying to look at earlier which is 15435, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As I mentioned, this is communication from Major Ljubisa Petricevic from the command of the 1st Igman Infantry Brigade to the SRK command, dated the 15th of January, 1995, and it's in response to an order from the SRK command. If you look halfway down the first page, you can ignore what were originally handwritten annotations, and there's a reference to the training which was carried out fully in 1994 in the organisation of the SRK. According to the operations report, the following officers were sent for training. It gives lists of the officers, and it says "for sniper squad commander 5." Could you enlighten us as to what the position you understand to have been in this particular part of the SRK in respect -- just -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In a regular sniper platoon, you will have several sniper pairs, so couples of snipers, and they will be commanded by an NCO or an officer who acts as both the advisor to the higher level, so battalion level, but also to -- to give orders to the -- to the sniper couples. So he acts as a -- as their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if there's a reference to five sniper squad commanders, how many snipers does that suggest?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I presume that if a sniper squad would have three or four pairs, so six to eight people, and five sniper instructors would have 30 to 40 -- 30 to 40 snipers under them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that that be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1615.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the document, which is still on your screen, in the introductory part of the document it says: "With reference to your document, Strictly Confidential 20/04-10/1, of 15th January 1995, which reached the 1st Igman Infantry Brigade on 14th January 1995." Your Honours, it obviously doesn't make any sense, so I'd like to put to you another document which was not on the notification filed which clarifies that reference. I'd like to call up, at this stage, 15412, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document which is about to arrive on our screens is an order from the SRK command: Strictly Confidential 20/04-10/1, dated the 5th of January, 1995. Therefore it appears that the previous order contained a typographical error. Where it said the 15th of January, it should have said the 5th. Now, if you can just look, Mr. Van der Weijden, at subparagraph (d), at the bottom of this -- of the page in front of you in English. It's also on this page in the B/C/S. Could you focus in on that subparagraph, Mr. Van der Weijden, and give us your observations on that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It would appear that the candidates were not just appointed but they were selected to train as instructors or coaches, because there's a clear selection of -- of people instead of just appointing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And just looking at the -- if you could focus on the top of -- at the part of this document which says: "Forward to all brigades, regiments, independent battalions of the SRK, IKM, and PKM of the SRK." Reading this document in conjunction with the previous document, are you able in any way to estimate on the number of sniper instructors which may have been taken for training?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly how big the brigades or the regiments were, because they can be full or half full, but it would be, well, at least over a hundred in total, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that that be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Since the Prosecution has been very good with us about admitting documents for which we've not given them notification, I don't see any reason why we can't reciprocate in this instance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted as Exhibit P1616.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up, now, document 06859.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your experience in the work which you have carried out, how is an individual sniper controlled by the overall command of the army? How does that work in -- in the units that you've served in? Just as a general matter. No need to look at the document at the moment.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The sniper, while regularly a soldier which would be -- which could have the same rank as a sniper, will have to go through all levels from individual group, platoon, company, battalion, brigade, and so forth. The sniper would already be at battalion level. So he would be already directly controlled [Realtime transcript read in error "volunteered"] at a higher level than the regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at this document and see if it assists you in providing comments on how snipers were controlled in this military environment. Now, I'd like to take you -- this document is from the SRK command, dated 15th of August, 1994, and it's been sent to the VRS Main Staff intelligence security sector. On the first page of the document, as you can see, it concerns the implementation of an anti-sniper agreement, and there is plan which will involve a joint staff consisting of representatives of UNPROFOR, the VRS, and the ABiH. Now, on the next page of the document, which will be on your screen for the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, it was from the security and intelligence sector of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you look at the -- one-third way down the document, Mr. Van der Weijden, we can see there, according to General Tolimir's instructions: "We would like to put forward our opinion and propose the following: "1. Sniping is only -- is to be stopped only by orders in the inner organisation and accordingly by taking of adequate measures. "2. As we've already explained, we cannot accept anti-sniper units which would operate on the respective side because it is not part of UNPROFOR's mandate, and a joint staff is not necessary because elaborate instruments of mutual information already exist." Under -- it goes on, under number 3, to suggest that there's no need for UNPROFOR to be present during the arrests or neutralisation of snipers. Does this -- can you provide any comments about the control over snipers from this entry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: First I would like to have something rectified at 34:43. It says here that since it would already be directly volunteered at a higher level; "volunteered" should be changed to "controlled," please. And then in regards to the instructions, the first sentence, the sniping is to be stopped only by orders in the inner organisation and accordingly by taking of adequate measures, it would be that the sniping is considered important enough for outside organisation not to interfere in that matter. And for sentence three, the arrest or neutralisation, well, I assume that neutralisation is a euphemism of eliminating of snipers. But, otherwise, I don't have any other comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that that be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document is 15741, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is from Major-General Dragomir Milosevic of the SRK command, and it's being sent to all units of the SRK, and it sets out the recipients of this order. It says pursuant to the order of the VRS Main Staff, strictly confidential, of 1st October 1995, and it suggests that this concerns the stopping of sniper fire on the town. And under number 1, could you have a look at that, paragraph 1, and give us your comments on that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The general clearly prohibits any sniper fire on the town of Sarajevo, but because there it says "until further notice," it might have happened before that time. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What about the chain of -- chain of control down to individual snipers? How does that work here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, the -- all levels are considered to be responsible for their sub-units, by this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you look at subparagraph 4 and provide your comments about that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It further amplifies the first sentence because he holds all unit commanders responsible, personally responsible, to withhold sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that that be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1618, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you an few general questions about your report. On page 4 of your report, you discuss the question of judging distance. I won't be showing you any particular documents at this stage. Why is judging distance particularly important for a sniper?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Judging distance is considered one of the main subjects of -- of any sniper course because it's not just the -- shooting is not just the rifle; it's -- it's a complete system in which you have the distances connected to the path of the bullet. And since the bullet doesn't fly a straight line, as -- just the sight will have, it flies a parabolic curve. So in order to be able to hit the target exactly where you want to hit, you will have to match the distance with adjustments of your scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, going back to the period of 1992 to 1995, could you describe the kind of information which a sniper crew would have available to it in order to judge distance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The most precise means would be just by maps. Nowadays laser rangefinders are in wide use, but at that time they were very new. Aside from maps, instruments that might have been used, I believe that in artillery crews, rangefinders have been used for quite a long time. That might have been borrowed or just asked for an observer to measure some distances. And besides from that there are -- there's a formula. Most military binoculars have an reticle which you can use to calculate the distance. It's not exact, but it gives a -- it's -- it's good enough to get a -- to get an accurate distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Focusing on a relatively static situation where the front lines remain more or less unchanged for weeks or months at an end, can you comment on the opportunities for a sniper or a sharpshooter to judge distance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Given -- given time and, of course, the technical situation, but if there's -- if it's safe enough for the sniper to shoot just at any -- any target, he can have target practice and from that target practice conclude the settings of his scope for future shots at that same distance. So for instance, he can use a clearly identifiable brick in a house or traffic sign that he can use to -- for target practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your report you refer to the use of machine-guns in several of the incidents. Now -- and you refer to the use of scopes on a machine-gun. What kind of magnification would -- would a scope on a machine-gun have in your experience?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, according to my experience and also the documentation, the typical scope would have a 4x amplification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Again looking at a fairly static situation, what measures would a machine-gun crew take to improve the accuracy of the weapon when firing over a couple of hundred metres?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, especially in a static situation, a machine-gun is far more effective if -- if it's placed on a tripod and then weighted down with sandbags. So then it's very effective to a -- much more over than a kilometre. So almost to 1500 metres you would be able to have relatively accurate fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your report you refer, and just now you've again referred to the use of binoculars, and you also in your report refer to a spotter scope with 20x magnification and the rifle scope which, as you've said, often has 4x magnification. Could you explain to the Court how a sniper team uses, first, the binoculars; second, the spotter scope; and third, the rifle scope in identifying a target.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I will explain -- try to explain for targets that are -- are at a longer distance. It's difficult for the -- for the eye -- of course, we would have a 1x magnification, but the eye is very suitable for detecting movement. If I would see movements, I would then switch to binoculars to try to get a reference as to where the target might appear. But then for -- to identify the target, I would have to switch to a 20x magnification. Using that 20x magnification, I could direct the sniper next to me with -- with the rifle with the 4x or higher magnification onto that target because he might not be able to get a good reference. So the 20x magnification is used for identification but also to talk the sniper, the shooter, onto the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is the procedure you've just described, is that exclusive to highly specialised and highly trained military snipers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, not really. It's also used for -- for hunting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you imagine that a static -- in a static situation a gunner crew, even if they're not trained snipers, on the basis of your experience would you imagine they might use the same instruments?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, they might use binoculars. They probably would use binoculars but not spotting scopes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on page 4 of your report you discuss the question of rules of engagement. Now, focusing on the rules of engagement that you've used or that you're familiar with from the Dutch or NATO exercises in which you've participated, could you tell the Court what those rules of engagement say about sniping at a person who appears to be a civilian? In what circumstances is that permitted?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, sniping would only be permitted if that civilian would pose an immediate threat to -- to yourself or to comrades.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What criteria would you take into account in determining if a civilian poses an immediate threat?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If that civilian would have a gun or maybe he would be busy with explosives, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if you're not sure that a target poses a threat, what do the rules of engagement normally require?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: There's no use of force allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the system that you've operated in, what are the consequences for shooting a civilian?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Court martial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your report -- we've discussed the general part of your report, and in your report you consider the origin of fire and the weapon used in 17 specific incidents and you provide your observations as to the opportunity the shooter would have had to identify the target as a combatant. Now, when did you visit the incident sites?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I visited some of the incident sites in November 2006 and some of the incident sites in January 2007 -- 2009, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What effect did the passage of time have on your ability to make a judgement about the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Aside from the construction of -- of new buildings and of the -- growing of the -- of the foliage around -- in the area, not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Because it's -- the lines of sight which are very important in my -- in my report, they were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe your methodology. When you arrived at an incident location, how did you make a judgement as to where fire would probably have come from?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would be taken to the exact incident site by the investigator, check the location with the data for which I had -- was given a GPS coordinate with my GPS, then reading the incident itself, determine where the victim was shot. So if it's -- if it's a leg wound or a chest wound or a head shot; if it's a leg wound, I would go down to the level at which the bullet might have -- would have entered and then look at the surroundings where -- where there's a clear line of sight to a suitable shooting position. Then in -- after visiting that incident site, I would go to the shooting positions that I had -- that I had identified and see if they were technically suited for -- to be able to be fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You were provided with witness statements which make -- in which the witnesses sometimes suggest origin of fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What effect did those statements have on your own determination of the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain your answer a little.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I -- the method that I employed is as I've stated before, so I took it for granted what -- what they said was the origin of fire. And first I saw if it was possible to be fired upon by that location. If it was the same, of course, then I would -- then I would assume that the position was the same as they -- as they implied, but otherwise -- yeah. Sometimes in my report the location they state and what I think is possible, they don't coincide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So were you -- were you being led by the witness statements, or were you exercising your independent judgement in each case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: My independent judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you did not undertake a comprehensive review of medical documentation nor obviously was the victim in loco when you carried out the your investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In some of the incident sites, the victim was present. But I didn't see the wounds or the scars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. And what -- what effect did the absence of the victim's body, for example, have on your ability to make a determination as to origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: From my point of view, again, not much, since I strictly look at the lines of sight. The distance are -- the distances from which I believe the victims were hit, they were at several hundred metres to -- to -- almost to a kilometre, and -- yeah. So in my opinion, it didn't really matter that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to return to your expert report at this stage, and that's 14045. And I understand you want to make one typographical correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So if we could look at page 63 on the e-court version. It's page 62 on the paper version. I note that Mr. Van der Weijden has his report in front of him in hard copy. I just want to inform the Court of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on that page, if you look at the second diagram on that page, Mr. Van der Weijden, the -- both of the distances are stated to be 616 metres. And I understand that where it says "Tomb from here to incident site 616 metres," that should read "550 metres;" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct. I would also like to say that on the second photo in which -- the bottom one, the circle where the sign leads to the "Tomb from here to incident site," the tomb was marked by a dark roof with a white wall, which is also visible in the top photograph which is marked 550 metres, just to support the change of distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we turn now to page 32 in e-court of the report. It's page 31 on the hard-copy version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your introductory paragraph here, Mr. Van der Weijden, you refer to the sniping of Tarik Zunic, a boy aged 14, who was walking home from school along Sedrenik Street and just past the streets -- screens which had been erected to provide some protection from snipers. You recall your assessment of this incident.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up document 11357.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document coming up is dated the same date as the incident you've described, 6th of March, 1995. It's an UNMO daily sitrep for the 6th of March, 1995. At page 3 of that document in the English, we see, under subparagraph (a)(iii): "Civilian male, aged 14 years, injured by SA RD in the left forearm at 061350 A MAR 95," and it gives a grid reference. It says the origin of fire is assessed by UNMOs at location as Sharpstone, and it gives another grid reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Van der Weijden, could you focus your attention on subparagraph 3(b), which begins with the words "During the activity in the area of Sharpstone." And it refers to the incidents in paragraph (a) of this report, including the incidents we've just looked at in subparagraph a -- 8(a)(iii), and it says: "During the activity in the area of Sharpstone ..." It goes on to say: "The Egybat anti-sniping APC at that location returned fire onto BSA positions on Sharpstone. Following this retaliation, UNMO Vogosca team received a telephone call from the CDR Radava BN." And it goes on to say, stating that: "If the Egybat APC in his target practice area (Sedrenik) is not removed within 30 minutes, it will be fired upon." Now, Mr. Van der Weijden, you've discussed the concept of target practice earlier in your evidence. Could you provide your comments on the reference to target practice there.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, the commander clearly sees that area as a target practice area where target practice is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the location that he's referring to is the area of Sedrenik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you -- that's the area in which the boy was shot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like that to be admitted, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This UNMO report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And it's just 10.00, Your Honours. I'd now request that the report of Mr. Van der Weijden be admitted under seal for the moment, as it refers to a number of protected witnesses. We will prepare a public version in due course. That's 65 ter 14045.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll admit it under seal for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That ends the direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no associate exhibit with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, there actually are some -- a number of documents which -- which have already been admitted in evidence which are relevant to his report. I could put them on the record right now, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if they've already been admitted, I don't see any reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can read the documents, and I'm not sure whether it would be of any assistance just now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, now is your time, your turn, to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Mr. Karadzic, we'll give a separate number for the public version of the report of this witness, which will be Exhibit P1621. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to knew topics, Mr. Van der Weijden, could we please just go back to your last commentary on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull up the last document that the Prosecutor called, P1619, on the monitors. P1619.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the document, Mr. Van der Weijden, have you noticed that the Egyptian Battalion opened fire on Serb positions on Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: According to this report they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Following that, the commander of the Serb unit demanded that that Egyptian Battalion transporter be removed from that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Gaynor tried to suggest to you that the Serb position wanted them removed so that they could open fire. Wouldn't it be more logical to conclude that the Serb side actually demanded that that APC be removed because it had opened fire on Serb position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would not be able to state that because, in a few lines above, the Egyptian anti-sniping APC at that location returned fire. So that would suggest that they were fired on before that. So the Egyptians didn't open fire, according to this report, they returned fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what if the Serbs had not opened fire from Spicasta Stijena and the Egyptian Battalion actually opened fire on Spicasta Stijena. What would have transpired in that case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are going too far. Let's come to your points, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So to wrap up with this document, Mr. Van der Weijden, do you know that we, the Serb side, actually felt that the Egyptian Battalion was biased and that it was in favour of the Bosnian side because they were Muslims too and that we were suspicious or -- suspicious of their getting closer to our lines?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to thank you for your willingness to meet with the Defence team, because it was very useful both to us and I believe to Mr. Gaynor as well, in order to spend as little time as possible on subsequent clarifications. To me it was very significant, your introductory remarks about snipers, and if you recall, we established that there were certain differences between the policies on snipers in NATO countries and in armies of other countries, including the Yugoslav People's Army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we've agreed that in NATO country armies sniper units acted independently and were employed at the request of other units, whereas within the Yugoslav People's Army, snipers existed as parts of each unit, not as a separate unit, but as members of those units.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In -- in NATO armies, the snipers do not act independently. They act -- there are smaller units, but they're still under control because independent is -- they're not completely independent, of course. And not only at the request of other units. They are structured at battalion level, but they can be requested by sub-units to be added to their unit. But for the rest, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have also agreed that the training of snipers was very important and that it was very -- a very important aspect of that was that you couldn't create instant snipers, that training snipers took a certain time; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The document which you've been shown, where the order of General Milosevic was mentioned of 1995 regarding sniper training, now, in respect of that document, would you agree with me that if such an order is issued that would mean that there was a need for training snipers? In other words, that they had not been trained up until then.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If it's the same document that we've been shown before, it was about sniper instructors not about snipers themselves, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But certainly that would imply that there would need to be training, sniper training, because sniper instructors are a significant -- a key element in that; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any evidence that that sniper training had actually been conducted as ordered by General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have established, and I thank you for enlightening me, we have established that there is a significant difference between sharpshooters and snipers; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: There is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can also see from your introductory remarks what the duties of a sniper are and that most frequently snipers operate behind enemy lines where they are supposed to keep low and open fire as required; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. Objection, Mr. President. The -- if Mr. Karadzic is going to refer to an assertion made by the witness in his report, I'd request that he point us to exactly the sentence that he's talking about, specifically the assertion that most frequently snipers had -- operate behind enemy lines. If he could point to the part of the report where that is asserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In paraphrasing, Mr. Karadzic, you need to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I will try to locate that part. And as soon as I do, I will advise you thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me reformulate that. Do you agree with me that we have agreed that Serb snipers in the area of Sarajevo did not cross the lines and act behind enemy lines? Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I've agreed that it was difficult to -- to cross the lines because it was static warfare, but I do not know if they did not cross the lines at all. But it was difficult -- it must have been difficult to cross the lines because of the static warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have agreed that there is a significant difference between a sniper -- a detached sniper operating behind enemy lines and ordinary soldiers or shooters who operate from a formation; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I -- I have never written in my report that the sniper, they operate between -- behind enemy lines. That's the general thought of the public, and an image is shaped by movies, because a sniper, he operates within his own lines or just in a no man's land. So between the lines. But there is big difference between a sniper and an ordinary soldier; yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have agreed that an ordinary soldier who is deployed on the front line sometimes open -- opens fire out of fear that he will be hit, as opposed to a sniper situation where if a sniper opens fire, then he would place himself in jeopardy, whereas an ordinary soldier is -- the situation is quite the opposite; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. President, what Mr. Karadzic appears to be doing here is putting to the witness his recollections of a meeting attended by the witness and Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Sladojevic and myself on Friday. Obviously Your Honours don't have any record of that. The witness -- instead of asking the witness does he agree to something and come out with a long paragraph of what he believes the witness may have said in that meeting, I suggest it's far more appropriate for Mr. Karadzic to frame short, specific questions asking the witness today does he agree with something or not, rather than referring to a meeting which is not in evidence anyway. And to keep his -- his questions short and focused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. While he's entitled to cross-examine the witness and also to put -- also able to put leading questions. It's much better -- you will be better off following the advice of Mr. Gaynor, Mr. Karadzic. Try to make your question simple and direct. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Could you reformulate your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to point you, Mr. Van der Weijden, to page 6 of the document, page 6 of 106, paragraph 3: [In English] "The big psychological difference however between regular infantry and snipers lies in the killing. Most of the kills made by regular infantrymen are in situations where it really is 'him or me.' If they don't kill, chances are high that they themselves will be killed. This means you can always justify it to yourself as self-defence. This makes it easier to emotionally deal with the fact that you are -- have killing a human being." Next paragraph is: "For snipers it is different." [Interpretation] And then you further go on to explain why and what the difference is with snipers. And then the next is sentence: [In English] "The enemy is at a safe distance. He will be in a concealed and safe position a little away from the front line. One could even say that in shooting he actually risked his life." [Interpretation] I apologise for having to shorten my questions, but that's only because I don't have enough time. So would you agree with me that, what you've said here, that an ordinary soldier has to shoot out of a fear that he would be shot, whereas a sniper is detached and that it would be better for him not to open fire otherwise he would be detected?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would -- I would like to state first that these are my personal observations, which are the subjects I have discussed with -- with colleagues throughout the years, but I do agree that for -- for snipers the shooting is different from the regular infantry soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now to return to my question. Were you aware of the deployment of forces and the confrontation lines within the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Only in very broad lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the confrontation lines were quite close? They were between 10 to 15 metres, one from the other, in the city itself. Did anyone tell you about it? I know you weren't there yourself, so did anyone tell you that the lines of the two opposing sides were so close to each other?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I am aware that -- I am aware that in some places the opposing sides were actually on both sides of the street facing each other. So at very short distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, you go on to say: [In English] "When a trained sniper takes his shot, he has entered something often described as 'the bubble.' This means he has temporarily blocked himself from anything that might keep him from hitting his target. So when a sniper shoots, it is always a deliberate attack with the intention to kill or wound the enemy." [Interpretation] Do you agree with me that Serb shooters or snipers, and we will clarify that later on, in order to reach some of these targets they would have to be either close to the separation line on -- or on the very separation line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: As I've stated, I wasn't -- I'm not aware of the exact separation lines of all locations. So I would not be able to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you agree that there is a difference between a person shooting from the separation line and the classic-case sniper? You could agree with me, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, the sniper can be behind the separation line, on the separation line, or a little before it. So I don't really understand the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I'm trying to have you tell us: If there is a difference between a sniper and a sniper's conduct and the soldier on the separation line, do you think that it was necessary for them to inform you on how far the separation line was from the alleged source of fire, sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because my method was not on which of the side has fired but strictly, purely, where the shot might have come from. So I did not look if it were a Serb or a -- or Muslim lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to that later on, but for now I would like to establish the following: whether it was a formation soldier shooting from the line of separation or a sniper who opened fire deliberately. So would it have been of help if you had known where the separation lines were and how far they were from the place from where the fire was opened?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In some incidents, it would have been of help because it would have made the judgement of a -- the tactical situation easier. Sorry, it would be not "technical" but "tactical."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it be important to establish whether fire was opened by a sniper or an ordinary soldier who would open fire in the other situation in order to avoid being killed himself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, because I've never established that any shot was fired by a sniper. So it doesn't -- for me, it doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that all these incidents were cases where some projectiles had come in, but it was never established that they were actually fired by snipers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: My methodology is -- has been to establish from where the sniper -- the shot might have come from, what kind of bullet was used, what -- in combination with weapon, and the distance. If you have a precision rifle in combination with a long distance, probably it would have been a sniper, but not conclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we go on break, I would like to clarify something. So the situation was the following: You were brought to a certain place and you were told where the fire was opened from. You were told either by the OTP investigators or by a witness. So what was then your course of action? Could you tell us, was it your task to tell them whether it was possible that a bullet had come from that direction or to ascertain that it had actually come from that direction, that position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Neither of those. It was my task to establish, in my view, where a bullet might have come from, from any direction. No matter what the implied origin of fire was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was it who determined the direction?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Based on the layout of the -- of the incident site. In -- in the layout of the incident site, the possibility of the -- the tactical possibilities of some of the locations from -- which were tactically possible and thereby eliminating more and more possibilities to eventually come out with a -- with an area that I think the shot came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll have a break, Mr. Karadzic, for 20 minutes. And we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, can you please help us to understand and grasp the methodology of your reaching conclusions. Who provided the coordinates to you of the alleged sites from which the fire originated and -- and the direction of the fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was not given any coordinates of alleged sites from which the site [sic] originated. I was only given coordinates from the incident sites where the victims were. But for the methodology, to explain it, I would -- it would help if I could draw a picture anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that would have been feasible if we had enough time. Let's move on and then see if we will have time later. So you received coordinates of the incident site. Who gave you those coordinates?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was given those coordinates by the OTP, by the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who suggested to you the site of the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: They were stated in -- sometimes in the incident of the -- the short description of the incident or by witness reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the provider who furnished this information?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you allowed for a possibility that the fire had come from any party involved, or were -- was it suggested to you that you focus on the Serbian positions only?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was allowed for any possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In our conversation, you said that the position of the victim is not always crucial for your task, and I also suppose that the same applies to the entry-wound channel, et cetera. Would you agree that just like any other point in a physical space has a surrounding area of 360 degrees?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if you exclude some 359 or 350 degrees and you decided to focus on the 10 degrees from which the alleged fire had come, and if you didn't have the position of the victim and the wound channel, you didn't have information about that, how did you reach your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Purely by looking at the layout of the incident site. So if for -- if the victim would be, for instance, in an enclosed garden with only one exit, the bullet can only have come through that exit. So that's how I came to a certain direction. In one incident, there is also still a mark of the impact of a bullet within -- on a wall, and that, together with a limited view on -- on the incident site, that leads back to the possible position of a shooter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, did you visit the site of the alleged fire, and did you observe the incident site from the site of the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Where possible, I have. And that was for the majority of the -- of the incidents. And I did observe the -- from the location where I think the shot came from, the location of the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many such locations relating to certain incidents did you observe? One or more than one?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: More than one. Out of the 15 to -- out of the 17 incidents of -- out of my head, I think about 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But speaking about an isolated incident, how many sites have you tested as possible sites from which the fire came?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I would not say about a site. I would -- it would be more an area. I would go -- from the incident site, I took -- I would calculate where the shot might have originated from, then go to that area and just walk through the area and scout several of -- possible locations. So they could be from -- from 1 to 20 to 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Out of these 20 to 50 locations, how many of them did you visit?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, if the -- in -- for one incident, if there's a trench along a long line and I see on -- I stop on four -- on four places along the trench and I see that I can observe the incident site from that location, I assume that from the -- the complete area is suitable for a position. So I stopped at as many locations as were possible for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 2007 or thereabout, were there still trenches in the town area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In some locations, yes. Signs of trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if you went to a location for which you assumed that the shot had come from, did you know the deployment of the troops, the distance of the lines, and all the other elements relating to this specific location? For example, where the trenches were, the deployment, the separation line, and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, because it's already a long time ago, it's, of course, very vague. But if I go to a location and I see bunker sites before that trench line, so from my military experience I can establish some positions from -- from that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the investigation information provided by the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina of any help to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Because of the -- the reports. They were not very complete. They only had a picture of a certain bullet in one case. So they were not -- they were not very helpful to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that at the time when the incident happened an investigation was indispensable for a legal processing of that incident and that the forensic and criminal investigation of the location would be most valuable and helpful in your drawing your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Not necessarily so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For how many incidents did you have investigation reports at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would have to check in my report, but I believe for about four to five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But these were incomplete; is that right? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move to individual incidents, Mr. Van der Weijden, let us clarify one issue. Therefore, your task was to establish the possible origin of a shot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you every able to reach a definitive conclusion, beyond reasonable doubt, the exact location from with the bullet had come from; and if you did, based on what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was never able to reach a definitive conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move to incident number 1 that you dealt with. That's an incident that happened at Sirokaca Street on the 13th of December, 1992. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's F1 from the list of sniper incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court 65 ter 10060.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, let us remind ourselves that a 3-year-old girl, Anisa Pita, was wounded in this incident. When she was wounded, she was playing on the veranda on the Zagrici Street; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: According to the witness statement it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which witness are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, it -- I don't know exactly who gave the witness statement, but it would either be the victim itself -- herself or her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this photograph, is the balcony on the right-hand side the balcony where the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, it's not. The balcony which is outlined, that is not incident -- the location. From where the picture was taken, that's the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this building and the balcony where the incident happened is shown in this photograph? And I'm talking about the place where this child was.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Could you -- just a moment. As far as I remember, the photo was taken from the exact location where the child was. So the photographer is standing on the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, this balcony where the photographer was standing is actually the place where the child was at the time when the incident happened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here that there is a direction marked here with the term Baba; is that correct? Is that where Baba is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would not be able to conclude that from this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it be helpful if you were told that a witness had indicated that this is the direction where the Baba Rock is from which the bullet came, and the witness is the mother's child?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It would be of no influence on my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you deal with the site where the shooting took place? What did you use as a basis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I used as a basis to go down to the level where I presume the shot has entered the victim. So if it's a 3-year-old child, I would go down to knee level, and from knee level I would observe the -- the surroundings to look for locations or gaps where -- where a shot might have come from. And since the garden is almost completely enclosed, it only offered a view of a location higher up the mountain, which later I did understand that it was Baba Rock. And that led me to the conclusion that it must have been -- come from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So does that correspond to the direction that is marked in the photograph? You have an arrow and the word "Baba."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would not be able to conclude this from this photo. I can't remember the exact vision I have in my head, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any material in your report that would be helpful for you to determine that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I think I do. On page 15 of the document. Page 15 in paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that later, because you're unable to make any markings at the moment, and therefore we shall not tender this photograph. But you did say that the photographer was standing at the place where the child had been standing. Can you please mark this exact position. And I would kindly ask the Registry to help you with the marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the point of this witness marking this photo, having no knowledge where the witness was, himself? We cannot admit this picture as it is confirmed by the witness this is the place where witness was allegedly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness has confirmed that the photographer was shooting a photograph from the place where the child was, and I deem that to be a sufficient reason to be admitted. Maybe he can mark it with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can admit this, but I was wondering what point there would be for the witness to mark this photo. Can you mark the place where the victim was at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not possible, because then the photographer would have to take a picture of -- of his feet, because he's -- the exact location is not in the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to tender this picture, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D637, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The date of picture seems to appear on the photo itself, Mr. Gaynor. You do not object to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have no objection to its admission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have in e-court 1D02402.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this particular section of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I do recognise some features, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I suggest to you to try and mark with number 1 the Baba Rock, then with number 2 the Muslim cemetery above Zagrici Street, and with number 3 Zagrici Street itself.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please put a date on this image and your initials.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the separation line was in this area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now call up 1D2406. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, may I remind you that this is the same building from the previous photograph on the left and that in the background one can see the Muslim cemetery. Do you see the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with a circle or use an arrow, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, this photograph was taken by the investigation team of the Defence with relation to the direction where the Baba Rock is located. On the right-hand side is the building where the incident took place, and this is a passage that leads to Baba.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the last sentence or the request for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, interpreters were not able to hear the last word of yours, your request to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just ask the witness to put the date and his initials on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Van der Weijden, you agree with the accused that this is -- the right-hand side is the building where the incident took place, and this is a passage that leads to Baba?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the last part, I cannot conclude. To the right side, a few metres to the right, is, indeed, the location of the house of the victim; but the direction that I'm looking in the photo, where the Muslim cemetery is, is not exactly the same direction as Baba Rock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
